items.prompt: An organization wants one integration surface for several Claude clients written in different languages. It needs typed tools, resources, prompts, capability negotiation, and independently evolving approved servers. Which mechanism fits?
constraints: Multiple clients need one typed lifecycle and capability protocol.
Servers should evolve independently while clients discover supported capabilities.

options.text: Copy private HTTP wrappers and schemas into each client so every language can tailor its integration independently.
Use a shared OpenAPI or JSON Schema catalog for typed operations, while each client implements its own lifecycle, resource, prompt, and capability-negotiation conventions.
Use MCP with clients and servers implementing the JSON-RPC lifecycle and relevant capability negotiation, tools, resources, and prompts.
Publish typed SDK bindings for each language and version them alongside the servers, with clients maintaining their own resource and prompt discovery behavior.

feedback.Reason: The requirements call for a shared typed protocol with lifecycle and capability negotiation across clients and servers. MCP provides that integration surface without duplicating private wrappers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: MCP uses a JSON-RPC client-server interaction with initialization and capability negotiation, and can expose tools, resources, and prompts through the protocol.
Details.scenarioApplication: Approved servers advertise supported capabilities and clients invoke typed tools or read resources through the common contract while each server evolves independently.
Details.errorCorrection: Choose an integration mechanism from interoperability and lifecycle requirements, not from the fact that every client can call an HTTP endpoint.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Protocol adoption adds implementation and versioning work, but it removes duplicated schemas and gives clients a common capability boundary.
Details.transfer: Use a shared protocol when several clients need typed discovery and independently managed capability servers; use a narrower direct interface for one deterministic caller.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: Private wrappers duplicate schemas and lifecycle behavior across languages and make capability evolution inconsistent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: OpenAPI or JSON Schema can type operations, but per-client lifecycle and discovery conventions do not provide the requested shared MCP negotiation for resources and prompts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: Per-language SDKs can be typed, but they duplicate lifecycle and capability behavior and make independently evolving servers harder to consume consistently.

items.prompt: A single internal dashboard needs one deterministic inventory lookup from an existing service with a stable typed API. No other client needs discovery or shared protocol features. What integration choice is proportionate?
constraints: There is one client and one deterministic operation.
The existing API already provides a typed contract.

options.text: Call the existing API through a narrowly scoped client tool, validate its response schema in the application, and defer MCP until shared protocol needs emerge.
Introduce MCP for the dashboard so even one deterministic lookup has lifecycle and capability negotiation, accepting the added protocol surface.
Replace the typed API with a CLI and parse human-readable output so the dashboard does not have to maintain a response schema.
Have Claude construct a direct database query when the API changes, bypassing the existing typed endpoint and its access controls.

feedback.Reason: The stable API already meets the one-client need. A scoped client tool preserves its typed contract and keeps the integration simple; MCP becomes justified when shared discovery or multiple clients require it.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Application-defined client tools execute structured calls and validate results at the application boundary, independent of a server protocol registry.
Details.scenarioApplication: Call the inventory endpoint with the required parameters, reject schema drift explicitly, and monitor the one integration until its requirements change.
Details.errorCorrection: Do not add a protocol lifecycle or discard a typed contract when the actual integration boundary is one deterministic operation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The dashboard will need a future migration if clients multiply, but the current path has lower complexity and a clearer failure surface.
Details.transfer: For a single stable API call, use the existing typed client boundary; adopt a shared protocol when interoperability and capability negotiation become real requirements.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: A new protocol adds lifecycle and capability machinery without a current interoperability or discovery problem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: Human-readable parsing discards the existing typed contract and makes schema errors harder to detect.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: Direct model-generated queries bypass the service contract and expand authority without solving the deterministic integration need.

items.prompt: A developer needs an interactive coding agent that runs tests, edits files, and works from a terminal on a remote server; the same commands must also work in shell scripts. Which integration boundary is appropriate?
constraints: The workflow needs process, filesystem, terminal, and scripting interaction.
Interactive and scripted execution must share the same command boundary.

options.text: Use a browser-only client and paste repository files into each request, then copy generated changes back to the remote server.
Use Claude Code's CLI for the terminal coding workflow and invoke it interactively or from scripts on the remote environment.
Delegate every test to a separate agent and have the coding client receive only natural-language pass or fail summaries.
Use one Messages API request containing the repository snapshot and ask Claude to return a complete patch without terminal access.

feedback.Reason: The required process, file, terminal, remote, and script interactions define a CLI boundary. Claude Code's CLI is designed for that interactive and scripted coding workflow.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A terminal CLI can read and modify the working tree, execute tests and commands, and be invoked directly or from automation with the same environment boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: Run the coding agent on the remote host, retain repository and test output, and use shell scripts for repeatable checks around the interactive session.
Details.errorCorrection: Choose the boundary that can perform and observe the required side effects; a text-only request cannot reproduce terminal workflow semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A CLI requires host setup and command permissions, but it preserves the process and filesystem context needed for realistic repository work.
Details.transfer: For coding agents that must edit files and run tools, integrate at the terminal or equivalent execution boundary rather than serializing the repository into prompts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: Browser copy and paste loses live process and filesystem access and cannot faithfully run the remote command workflow.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: Delegated summaries remove direct test and file context from the coding agent and make failures harder to reproduce.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: A snapshot request can return text but cannot execute tests, inspect resulting files, or support the required scripts.

items.prompt: A research lead delegates independent market questions to specialist workers. Each worker searches different sources and returns structured evidence; the lead synthesizes one report with explicit ownership. Which TWO integration decisions fit? Select TWO.
constraints: Workers need scoped objectives, source guidance, and structured handoffs.
One lead owns synthesis; a tool protocol alone does not define research coordination.

options.text: Use MCP as the only coordination mechanism and let workers infer their objectives from the available tools.
Use agent-to-agent orchestration with explicit worker objectives, source and output guidance, bounded assignments, and structured artifacts for the lead.
Give every worker the full conversation and ask each to return a complete final report for the lead to choose by prose quality.
Run one shared API call for all markets and let Claude simulate specialist ownership inside a single response.
Preserve worker ownership and evidence identifiers in each handoff so the lead can reconcile conflicts and cite the responsible source.

feedback.Reason: The workload is independent research with explicit ownership and a synthesis lead. Agent-to-agent coordination supplies objectives and handoffs; preserving ownership and evidence lets the lead reconcile rather than guess.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Workers receive bounded assignments and return structured artifacts, while a lead agent coordinates and synthesizes those artifacts after retrieval and source checks.
Details.scenarioApplication: Assign one market question per worker, require source and uncertainty fields, and join each artifact to the lead report and its citations.
Details.errorCorrection: Distinguish a protocol for calling tools from a coordination contract for independent agents and their final owner.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Agent coordination adds state, artifacts, and lead synthesis cost, but it reduces duplicated context and makes source responsibility explicit.
Details.transfer: For open-ended specialist work, define worker objectives and evidence handoffs, then preserve ownership through final synthesis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: MCP may expose tools but does not assign research objectives, ownership, or synthesis responsibilities.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: Full-history independent reports waste context and make conflict and source ownership harder for the lead to resolve.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: One response hides independent failure and ownership boundaries and cannot provide the requested worker handoffs.

omittedCorrectElementExplanationsByOptio.b: Without explicit agent objectives and structured assignments, workers cannot be coordinated or evaluated as independent research units.
omittedCorrectElementExplanationsByOptio.e: Without preserved ownership and evidence identifiers, the lead cannot attribute or reconcile conflicting findings.

items.prompt: Six clients need shared interactive access to typed tools, resources, and prompts, but a nightly ETL job must move millions of rows through an existing batch API with streaming and throughput guarantees. Which integration split is sound?
constraints: The interactive clients need shared protocol features.
The ETL data plane already has a high-volume batch contract.

options.text: Use MCP for the shared interactive capability surface and retain the direct batch API for ETL, returning bounded job status or artifacts rather than relaying every row through model context.
Replace batch streaming with an MCP tool that fetches and returns pages of ETL records, using the interactive clients to advance each page.
Replace the batch API with a CLI that emits text, then ask each interactive client to parse the output and emulate shared resource discovery.
Expose ETL artifacts as MCP resources and stream their chunks through resource reads, replacing the existing direct batch API with the interactive protocol.

feedback.Reason: MCP fits the shared interactive capability surface, while the existing batch API already satisfies the ETL data-plane contract. Forcing millions of rows through model context adds overhead without a discovery need.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: MCP can negotiate shared tools, resources, and prompts for interactive clients; the direct API preserves streaming and throughput for bulk transfer and can return an artifact or job status.
Details.scenarioApplication: Keep ETL records in the batch service, expose job status or a bounded artifact to the interactive surface, and use MCP for the six client capability interactions.
Details.errorCorrection: Select the protocol at each integration boundary instead of imposing one surface on workloads with different payload and throughput semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Two mechanisms require clear ownership and monitoring, but they avoid context pollution and preserve the proven bulk data path.
Details.transfer: Use shared protocol discovery for interactive capabilities and a direct typed data plane for high-volume transfer when their contracts differ.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: Page-by-page transfer through the interactive clients replaces the established batch streaming path without evidence that its throughput contract is preserved.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: A CLI does not provide the requested typed resources and capability negotiation and would replace a working batch interface unnecessarily.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: Resource reads can expose artifacts, but replacing the existing streaming API with an interactive protocol loses its measured bulk-throughput contract.

items.prompt:
Six clients in three languages need one shared remote capability surface with typed tools, resources, prompts, lifecycle negotiation, and independently deployed servers. A direct API wrapper works for one existing dashboard but cannot express server capability discovery across clients.

Which protocol choice fits this shared, evolving remote capability surface?
constraints: Six clients in three languages need one shared surface for typed tools, resources, prompts, lifecycle, and capability negotiation.
Servers deploy independently and clients may support different optional capabilities.
A direct wrapper works for one dashboard but cannot express shared discovery.

options.text: Call the existing typed API through separate client tools because direct calls are simpler for the first dashboard.
Use MCP for the shared negotiated surface, reserving direct APIs for isolated integrations without protocol needs.
Use an agent-to-agent handoff protocol for every tool call so clients can delegate capability discovery to one lead.
Define a custom JSON envelope around the existing dashboard API and add client-specific capability flags.

feedback.Reason: The decision is driven by shared protocol semantics and independent evolution rather than by language preference alone.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: MCP uses JSON-RPC with lifecycle and capability negotiation and optional resources, prompts, and tools. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The shared lifecycle and negotiated capability requirements reverse the single-client direct API choice.
Details.scenarioApplication: Use MCP for the shared client-server surface, implement the required lifecycle and capability negotiation, and keep direct API clients only for isolated integrations without those protocol needs.
Details.errorCorrection: Separate wrappers duplicate lifecycle and capability handling across six clients and cannot provide the requested shared optional surface.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the requirement collapsed to one deterministic dashboard lookup with no discovery or shared server evolution, return to the narrowly scoped direct API client.
Details.transfer: Route each information need through the smallest governed interface that matches its evidence shape, and preserve explicit authorization, freshness, and unavailable states when the evidence cannot support a claim.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: Separate wrappers duplicate lifecycle and capability handling across six clients and cannot provide the requested shared optional surface.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: A handoff pattern does not supply the requested shared tool/resource lifecycle and negotiated capability contract for independently deployed servers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: A custom envelope recreates lifecycle and negotiation independently and leaves six adapters to maintain incompatible capability semantics.

items.prompt:
Four remote clients use a shared MCP server over HTTP. Each tenant has distinct read and write scopes, the server advertises tools and resources during capability negotiation, and a client may not see an operation it cannot invoke.

Which protocol and authorization boundary should the shared HTTP server implement?
constraints: Four remote clients share one MCP HTTP server, but tenant read and write scopes differ.
Capabilities must be advertised per client, and a client must not see an operation it cannot invoke.
The resource server can enforce audience, tenant, scope, and invocation checks.

options.text: Use one broad direct API schema for every client and let the model decide which tenant operation is allowed.
Advertise every tool to every client and rely on an invocation-time denial when a scope is missing.
Use MCP HTTP with per-client capabilities and tenant scopes, and recheck authorization at invocation.
Use MCP for transport but bind all sessions to a shared tenant role because the server has one deployment.

feedback.Reason: The integrated protocol and auth requirements make a single unscoped wrapper insufficient while keeping application enforcement explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: MCP uses JSON-RPC with lifecycle and capability negotiation and optional resources, prompts, and tools. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Protocol selection and authorization are coupled here: the shared negotiated surface must preserve per-client capability and resource boundaries.
Details.scenarioApplication: Use MCP for the shared HTTP surface, advertise only supported capabilities per client, bind each session to its tenant and scopes, and recheck authorization at invocation.
Details.errorCorrection: A broad client surface leaks capabilities, and model choice cannot replace resource-server scope enforcement.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If all clients become one trusted local process with no optional capability or tenant separation, a direct typed API may be proportionate.
Details.transfer: Route each information need through the smallest governed interface that matches its evidence shape, and preserve explicit authorization, freshness, and unavailable states when the evidence cannot support a claim.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: A broad client surface leaks capabilities, and model choice cannot replace resource-server scope enforcement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: Invocation denial is necessary but late; the requirement also prevents a client from seeing operations it cannot invoke.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: Deployment identity does not remove tenant isolation; each session still needs its own tenant and read/write scope binding.
